beats.text: Wittgenstein believed most philosophy was a tangle caused by misusing language.
Language, he said, works by picturing facts in the world — things that are or aren't the case.
But the deepest things — meaning, value, God, the point of it all — aren't facts in the world.
So when we try to state them, our sentences quietly break. They gesture at what cannot be said.
That doesn't make them worthless. He thought they were the most important things of all.
They must be shown, lived, felt — not spoken. His book ends with a single, famous instruction.
"Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent."

source_note: Quote: Tractatus, trans. C. K. Ogden (1922, public domain).
